stops.name: Château de Bourlémont, born amid the tide
stops.campa: On the feast of the Kings a son is born to the lord of Bourlémont in the castle on its spur above the meeting of Meuse and Saônelle. France is swelling with a tide of spiritual energy centred on the power of youth: shepherd children carry letters from Christ, and the roads fill with singing. The child is named Joffrey. From the walls the household looks down the valley to Greux and Domremy, the family villages, and to the dark shoulder of the Bois Chenu. Everything this life will carry, the crib, the Rock, and the tree, lies inside that view or at the end of its roads.

stops.name: Domrémy, the infant lord and the pueri
stops.campa: On the day of the Lendit fair the shepherd Stephen of Cloyes stands at Saint-Denis with a letter given him by Christ in the guise of a pilgrim, and thousands of pueri gather to march for the sea. Far east on the Meuse, the infant lord is carried into Saint-Rémy of Domremy, the half of the village that answers to his father's house. The tide of the Children's Crusade never reaches the Vosges, but its stories do, and they will be told over his cradle for years: children walking to part the waters, a crusade of the small and the pure.

stops.name: The beech tree on the road to Vaucouleurs, the boy under the boughs
stops.campa: The boy grows on stories of Stephen of Cloyes and the great Crusade of the Children. On the road from his castle toward Vaucouleurs there is a field at the edge of the wood where a giant beech stands and a spring runs from the ground, and the children of Greux and Domremy gather there to dance. Joffrey rides beneath the boughs with a wooden lance, dreaming of leading pilgrims under the banner of the Rose Cross. This is his destiny, and the tree, which is older than his family's name, already seems to know it.

stops.name: Neufchâteau, the fair and the pilgrims' stories
stops.campa: At the Michaelmas fair of Neufchâteau, among wool merchants and returned pilgrims, the boy hears Outremer spoken of as a real place with real roads: Acre of the crowded harbour, the Sepulchre under its dome, the toll-gates of the Saracens. Grey friars of the new order of the Poverello have begun to pass through Lorraine barefoot, preaching penance: his mother's kin, the household whispers. Joffrey measures himself against the sea and finds he is not yet tall enough. He begins to wait, which is a kind of prayer.

stops.name: Château de Bourlémont, the departure at twelve
stops.campa: Joffrey has turned twelve, and Pierre takes his only son over the mountains to Italy, hoping the road will form him as the Caucasus once formed Pierre at his own father's side. Both are curious to meet the dirty friar, and Pierre judges it important that the boy know his older cousin, the son of Pica, and profit from the connection in his eventual crusade. They ride out from the castle gate in the October rains, the Meuse behind them, the white of the passes ahead.

stops.name: The Great Saint Bernard, over the mountain
stops.campa: Father and son cross by the pass of the Great Saint Bernard at Martinmas, between walls of early snow, and sleep at the hospice among merchants of Champagne and pilgrims bound for Rome. The monks' great dogs walk the drifts at dawn. Below, on the Italian side, the vineyards still carry leaves; Joffrey watches the light change as every northern child does, the south arriving like a warmer kind of truth. He carries his father's stories of the Caucasus the way his father once carried them: as a promise that the world is wide.

stops.name: Rieti, the valley of the hermitages
stops.campa: They come down the pilgrim roads into the valley of Rieti, where the Pope keeps court and the friar's hermitages hang in the oak woods. All the talk is of Francesco: Honorius has just sealed his Rule with a bull, and the friar has asked leave to make, for Christmas, a memorial of the child born at Bethlehem: to see with bodily eyes the hardships of his infant needs. Pierre and Joffrey turn aside from the Roman road toward the little mountain village of Greccio, following the mule tracks and the rumour of lanterns.

stops.name: Greccio, the first nativity
stops.campa: They arrive at Greccio on Christmas Eve. That night the mountainside fills with torches, and in a cave their cousin has prepared a beautiful recreation of the manger: many lanterns lighting the scene, an ox and an ass, men dressed as magi of far lands, a Virgin and a Joseph, and among the heaps of golden hay the child of Bethlehem. Joffrey, who will one day stand in Bethlehem itself, is struck to the heart by the poverty of his Lord's birthplace, seen now with his own eyes.

stops.name: Greccio, communion from the frail cousin's hands
stops.campa: In the morning father and son receive communion from the hands of friar Bourlemont. Pierre is pleased by the likeness of the magi to those he saw in his time with Nizami; he feels that something in the stories he told Pica has passed into her son, embodied now as art and faith, set into the world to be contemplated. He holds Joffrey's hand while waves of heat pour from his frail cousin in the midst of his prayer before the scene. The boy stores the warmth away; he will spend a lifetime giving it back.

stops.name: Château de Bourlémont, the boy who saw Bethlehem in a cave
stops.campa: They recross the passes in the spring thaw, and the boy carries the cave home with him like a coal carried in wet moss. That September, on the mountain of La Verna far behind them, the sky will open over their cousin and a seraph will descend; Joffrey will not hear that story for five years, and when he hears it he will be walking to Bethlehem. For now he is thirteen, and the Meuse valley receives him back with its ordinary rain, its dancing children, its patient tree.

stops.name: Marseille, taking the sea at sixteen
stops.campa: At sixteen he takes the sea. The Emperor's crusade has sailed and stalled, Frederick turned back to Brindisi with fever, and the Pope has excommunicated him for it, but the pilgrim ships still work out of Marseille, and Joffrey goes aboard among Champenois knights and grey friars bound for their Province of the Holy Land. The banner of his boyhood dream is rolled in his baggage. The city smells of pitch, salt and Saracen spices, and the sea is the largest thing he has ever seen.

stops.name: Saint-Jean-d'Acre, the Province of the Holy Land
stops.campa: He lands at Saint-Jean-d'Acre and is glad to find the brotherhood of friars founded by his cousin: the Province of the Holy Land, established by the son of Pica a decade before, the order's oldest mission field. In their poor house he is known at once, the boy of Greccio, kin of the founder, and the friars claim him as their own. Acre roars around them: Pisans, Genoese, Templars, caravans, forty tongues in one market. Joffrey waits, as all Outremer waits, to see what the excommunicated Emperor will do.
